vignette:
Martha is seventy-seven now, but she still wakes at three in the morning—the same time every night—and lies perfectly still in the dark, listening. Her bedroom is small, cluttered with photo albums and stacks of old books, but in the silence she can feel every shadow pressing in. She grips the edge of the blanket and forces herself to breathe. *Just a house.* She knows it’s just a house. But the muscles in her neck stay tight until the first gray light seeps through the blinds.

She was a school counselor for thirty-four years, mostly at a middle school on the outskirts of a quiet town. She loved the work—loved the kids who came to her office smelling of peanut butter and damp coats, who drew pictures of their dogs and cried over friend drama. She kept a box of tissues on her desk and a jar of peppermints. She thought she understood fear: the eighth grader terrified of a math test, the sixth grader whose parents were divorcing. She thought she could help.

Then one afternoon in early spring, a man she did not know walked past the front office and down the hallway with a rifle. She heard the first shot from her office—a sound like a metal chair being dropped, but wrong, too sharp. She stepped into the hall and saw a student lying on the linoleum. The boy was thirteen, Jacob, who had come to her just the week before about a bad grade. She ran toward him. She remembers the blood spreading under his backpack. She remembers pulling him into the doorway of her office, pressing her hand to his chest, telling him he would be okay. She remembers the shooter’s footsteps. Then the lockdown alarm. Then the police arriving.

She did not know until later that Jacob had died before the paramedics reached him. She stayed in the hallway for two hours, crouched beside that door, not letting go.

After the shooting, Martha tried to return to work. The school reopened six weeks later. She sat in her office, but the peppermints stayed in the jar. Every knock on her door made her flinch. She stopped eating lunch in the cafeteria because the echoing noise brought her back to the hall. She retired early, at sixty-three, telling herself she wanted to travel with her husband. They did travel—road trips to national parks, quiet weekends by a lake. She could smile. She could hold his hand. But at night she still heard the footsteps.

Her husband died four years ago. Now the house is very still. She avoids the middle school section of the grocery store. She cannot watch the news, especially not stories about schools. Once a neighbor asked if she would volunteer at the local elementary library, and Martha said yes automatically, then canceled the night before. She told the neighbor she had a cold. Actually, she sat in her recliner with the blinds closed, her stomach knotted, her heart banging against her ribs. She felt ashamed. She had been a helper. Now she could not even walk into a building full of children.

She still thinks about Jacob. Not every day—sometimes a week goes by, and then she will see a boy with a red backpack or hear a laugh that sounds like his, and her chest tightens. She replays the moment she pressed her hand to his chest, wondering if she pressed hard enough, if she should have turned him over, if she should have screamed for a nurse. She knows, intellectually, that she did what anyone would do. But knowledge does not live in the body. Her body lives in that hallway.

Last week a leaf blower started up outside her window, and she dropped a coffee cup. She stood in the kitchen, her hands shaking, before she understood what had scared her. She cleaned up the shards and told herself she was fine. But she did not sleep that night, either. She just listened, and waited, and remembered.
